entries.clue: Blood cells' origin is one male interred in burial mound (4,6)

indicators.note: something interred in a mound is buried inside it, so ONE M goes inside BARROW

blocks.note: a barrow is an ancient burial mound

annotation.surface: A grisly archaeology note: whatever produces blood cells turns out to be a man buried in an ancient tumulus.
annotation.walkthrough: A barrow is also a wheelbarrow, but 'burial mound' pins down the ancient earthwork. The apostrophe in 'cells'' belongs to the definition: the marrow is where the cells come from.
annotation.definitionFit: Bone marrow is the tissue inside bones where blood cells are made.

entries.clue: Feel bitter about pressure to avoid attending (6)

indicators.note: the P keeps away from the word, so it is removed

blocks.note: attending = present, as at a meeting

annotation.surface: Someone sore about being pushed to skip an event they would rather attend.
annotation.walkthrough: PRESENT loses its P to leave RESENT; 'pressure' is not a feeling here but the physics symbol.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the verb means to take something with bitterness or indignation.

entries.clue: His Excellency probes Byzantine prince in disguise (8)

indicators.note: byzantine means convoluted, so the letters of PRINCE are tangled
HE probes, pushing into the rearranged letters

blocks.note: HE is the abbreviation for His Excellency, an ambassador's title

annotation.surface: A diplomatic intrigue in Constantinople: an ambassador snooping on a Byzantine royal who is travelling incognito.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Byzantine' pretends to be the prince's nationality; it is the instruction to jumble PRINCE, with HE pushed in before the final R.
annotation.definitionFit: Turning a message into cipher hides its meaning from outsiders, a disguise for text.

entries.clue: Interfering sod led mobile to block online content (10)

indicators.note: mobile letters move about, so SOD LED is rearranged
the rearranged letters sit in the middle of MEME, blocking it

blocks.note: a meme is a joke image or phrase shared online

annotation.surface: An irritable complaint about some so-and-so using a phone to stop things being posted online.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Online content' looks like the thing being blocked by a filter; it is the outer word, split open. 'Sod' is a mild British insult, but here it only supplies letters.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone meddlesome is always interfering in other people's affairs.

entries.clue: Told I'm going to offshore location (4)

indicators.note: something told is spoken, so we want the word that sounds like I'LL

blocks.note: I'll is the contraction for I will, i.e. I'm going to

annotation.surface: Someone announcing a trip to an island.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface runs 'I'm going to' straight into the destination, so it reads as a travel plan rather than the phrase to be said out loud.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: an island is a place lying off the shore.

entries.clue: Directed Up or another Pixar movie in elaborate style (6)

indicators.note: in a down clue, letters directed up read from bottom to top, so OR turns round

blocks.note: Coco is a 2017 Pixar film, like Up

annotation.surface: A film-buff question: who directed Up, or some other Pixar film, in a lavish way?
annotation.walkthrough: Up really is a Pixar film, which is why it hides so well: in this down clue it is the instruction to turn OR round.
annotation.definitionFit: Rococo is the ornate eighteenth-century style of decoration.

entries.clue: French resort business to stock bara brith without crusts (8)

indicators.note: BIZ stocks the letters, holding them inside
each word of bara brith loses its outside letters, like bread with the crusts cut off

annotation.surface: A Welsh tea-shop firm stocking decrustified fruit loaf, somewhere on the French coast.
annotation.walkthrough: Bara brith is a Welsh fruit loaf. Both of its words are trimmed, and 'crusts' suits bread perfectly, which is why the instruction goes unnoticed.
annotation.definitionFit: Biarritz is a seaside resort on France's Atlantic coast.

entries.clue: Reported grain yield (4)

indicators.note: reported speech is heard, not read, so we want the word that sounds like SEED

blocks.note: a grain of wheat or barley is a seed

annotation.surface: A news item on the harvest: the reported crop of grain.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Grain yield' reads as one farming phrase, but it splits: grain is the sound, yield is the definition, a verb rather than the noun it looks like.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the sense of giving up or handing over, as a country does with territory.

entries.clue: Shrubs from Avon's source spreading over banks (9)

indicators.note: a river's source is where it starts, so the first letter of Avon
the letters spread out into a new arrangement

blocks.note: o = over, the cricket scoring abbreviation

annotation.surface: A river scene: bushes spreading along the banks from where the Avon rises.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Banks' pretends to be riverbanks, which the Avon makes natural; it is the financial kind. An over is a set of six balls in cricket.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by class: the plant is an evergreen, poisonous Mediterranean bush with pink or white flowers.

entries.clue: Sheepish climber gets oxygen first (5)

indicators.note: O comes first, before the climber

blocks.note: O is the chemical symbol for oxygen
a vine is a climbing plant

annotation.surface: An embarrassed mountaineer being handed an oxygen mask before anyone else.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Sheepish' pretends to mean embarrassed, and a climber on oxygen fits a mountain; but it means like a sheep, and the climber is a plant.
annotation.definitionFit: Ovine means of or like sheep, which is sheepish taken literally.

entries.clue: One fleeced by second person over the phone (3)

indicators.note: on the phone we only hear the word, so YOU gives its sound-alike

annotation.surface: A phone scam victim, swindled by someone on the other end of the line.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Fleeced' means cheated in the scam story, but a ewe is literally fleeced at shearing.
annotation.definitionFit: A ewe is a female sheep, one that has its fleece shorn.

entries.clue: Unicode sure to break eventually (2,3,6)

indicators.note: the letters are broken up and put back together differently

annotation.surface: A programmer's gloomy forecast that the Unicode text encoding is bound to fail sooner or later.
annotation.walkthrough: Unicode is the standard for encoding text on computers; the tech surface hides a very ordinary phrase.
annotation.definitionFit: In due course means eventually, at the proper time.

entries.clue: The Scarlet Letter, with long introduction from Hawthorne (5)

annotation.definitionNote: the definition is the letter H itself; AITCH is how that letter's name is spelt

blocks.note: in Hawthorne's novel The Scarlet Letter, Hester Prynne must wear a red letter A
to long for something is to itch for it

annotation.surface: A note on Hawthorne's novel The Scarlet Letter and its lengthy opening chapter.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Long introduction' reads as one phrase, a verdict on the novel's famously slow preface. Split it: long is ITCH, and the introduction of Hawthorne is its first letter, H.
annotation.definitionFit: The first letter of Hawthorne is H, and aitch is the name of that letter.

entries.clue: To sum up, most of epic is boring to me (9)

indicators.note: take most of the word, dropping its last letter
IS bores into TOME, sitting inside it

blocks.note: EPIC with its last letter deleted
taken as it stands, drilled into TOME between M and E

annotation.surface: A reader's verdict: in short, a long epic mostly bores me.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boring' looks like a complaint about the epic; it is the instruction to drill IS into TO ME. A tome, like an epic, is a heavy book, which is the surface's joke.
annotation.definitionFit: To epitomise something is to sum it up in a typical example.

entries.clue: Facing repercussions, won't air the broadcast (2,3,5)

indicators.note: broadcast means scattered widely, so the letters are scattered

blocks.note: anagram fodder, 10 letters; the apostrophe is ignored

annotation.surface: A TV station in trouble with the regulators refuses to air a programme.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Air' and 'broadcast' both sound like television, so the whole clue reads as a scheduling row; broadcast means scattered.
annotation.definitionFit: Someone in hot water is in trouble, facing the consequences of what they did.

entries.clue: Rider's request to cycle in surrounding area (10)

indicators.note: the first letter of REQUEST cycles round to the end
to surround something is to enclose it on all sides, so the word before it wraps around the one after

blocks.note: REQUEST with its R moved from front to back
taken as it stands, then split round A

annotation.surface: A horse rider asking to go for a bicycle ride round the neighbourhood.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Rider's' reads as possessive, but the 's is just 'is': the rider is the answer. 'Cycle' fits a rider but means the letters rotate.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym: the noun means a person who rides horses, from Latin equus, horse.

entries.clue: Trouper, playing loud man at National Theatre, leads in Zenda as "unconquered" villain (6,2,7)

indicators.note: the letters are played with, rearranged
the leading letters of the words that follow

blocks.note: first letters of Zenda, as, unconquered

annotation.surface: A veteran actor at the National Theatre in a stage version of The Prisoner of Zenda, playing a noisy undefeated baddie.
annotation.walkthrough: Rupert of Hentzau is the dashing villain of Anthony Hope's The Prisoner of Zenda, and gives his name to its sequel, so the theatrical surface points straight at him.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by example: he is the charming, treacherous antagonist of Anthony Hope's 1894 adventure novel.

entries.clue: Soldier at base, tackling onset of shellshock, gets to demobilise? (8)

indicators.note: LYE tackles the S, holding it inside
the onset of a word is its first letter

blocks.note: lye is a strong alkali, and an alkali is a base in chemistry

annotation.surface: A soldier in camp, suffering the first signs of shellshock, is about to be discharged.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Base' is a military base in the story but a chemical base in the wordplay. The question mark flags that 'demobilise' is used whimsically, to make immobile rather than release from the army.
annotation.definitionFit: To paralyse is to make unable to move, which is demobilise read literally.

entries.clue: Arrest man, reflecting on drug's designation (8)

indicators.note: a reflection shows things back to front, so MAN reverses

blocks.note: to nick is British slang for to arrest

annotation.surface: A police officer pondering what a drug is called before arresting someone.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Reflecting on' reads as thinking about; it is two instructions, reverse MAN and put it on the E.
annotation.definitionFit: A loose synonym: an informal name is one kind of designation, a label someone goes by.

entries.clue: Week wrestling with short set of exercises (9)

indicators.note: the letters grapple and tumble into a new order

annotation.surface: A fitness plan: a week of wrestling alongside a brief routine.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Short' looks like it trims something; it is just five letters of fodder, and 'set of exercises' is the definition, not a gym programme.
annotation.definitionFit: A definition by description: a school handout is a printed page of exercises for pupils to complete.

entries.clue: Poured out barrel containing whiskey (6)

indicators.note: SPEED holds the W inside it

blocks.note: to barrel along is to speed
Whiskey is the radio code word for W

annotation.surface: A cask of whiskey being emptied out.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Barrel' and 'whiskey' make a distillery; barrel is a verb, to go fast, and whiskey is just the letter W.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym in the past tense: the verb means gushed or poured out in a stream.

entries.clue: Asteroid captured by space researchers (5)

indicators.note: the answer is held inside the following words

annotation.surface: Astronomers catching an asteroid, perhaps with a probe.
annotation.walkthrough: The surface is so apt that 'captured' reads as a space mission; the asteroid is sitting in the letters of the next two words.
annotation.definitionFit: Ceres is the largest body in the asteroid belt.

entries.clue: Replace gear thief lifted (6)

indicators.note: in a down clue, lifted letters read upwards, so LOOTER turns round

annotation.surface: A thief has stolen some equipment and it needs replacing.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Lifted' is slang for stolen, which fits the thief perfectly; in this down clue it means turned upside down.
annotation.definitionFit: To retool is to replace the tools or equipment of a factory.

entries.clue: Quick transport announcement about shortened tram (6,5)

indicators.note: BULLETIN goes about, round, the letters
TRAM loses its last letter

blocks.note: a bulletin is an official announcement

annotation.surface: A public transport notice about a tram service being cut back.
annotation.walkthrough: The whole clue sounds like a travel update, and 'transport' and 'tram' both suggest the answer's field without giving it away.
annotation.definitionFit: A bullet train is a high-speed train, such as Japan's Shinkansen.

entries.clue: What tempts bishop with boundless faith? (4)

indicators.note: without its bounds, the letters at each end

blocks.note: b = bishop, as in chess notation
FAITH without its first and last letters

annotation.surface: A question about what could lure a bishop whose faith knows no limits.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Boundless faith' is the language of devotion, but boundless means the word loses its edges.
annotation.definitionFit: Bait is something used to tempt, as with a fish or a trap.

entries.clue: I appreciate that company's Mexican food (4)

blocks.note: ta is British informal for thank you

annotation.surface: A diner thanking a firm for its Mexican food.
annotation.walkthrough: 'I appreciate that' reads as a full sentence of thanks; its one-word British equivalent is TA.
annotation.definitionFit: A taco is a Mexican folded tortilla with a filling.

entries.clue: Pitch of backing singer (3)

indicators.note: going backwards, so RAT is reversed

blocks.note: an informer 'sings' to the police, and a rat is an informer

annotation.surface: A musical note about the key a backing vocalist sings in.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Pitch' and 'backing singer' make a recording studio; pitch is the black stuff, and backing is the reversal, not the choir.
annotation.definitionFit: Pitch is a black sticky substance like tar.

entries.clue: Header omitted from paper edition (5)

indicators.note: the header, the first letter, is left off

annotation.surface: A newspaper printed without its masthead.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Paper' and 'edition' suggest a newspaper, but the paper is tissue, which loses its T.
annotation.definitionFit: A plain synonym from publishing: each numbered release of a magazine or paper is an edition.

entries.clue: Drink loads in closing bars (5,4)

indicators.note: in means inside, so the loads are placed within the closing bars

blocks.note: a coda is the closing passage of a piece of music

annotation.surface: Heavy drinking just before the pubs shut.
annotation.walkthrough: 'Closing bars' pretends to be pubs at closing time; the bars are musical ones, and the drink is a soft one.
annotation.definitionFit: Cream soda is a vanilla-flavoured fizzy soft drink.
